summary.text: A storm surge is a rise in water above the normal tide level, usually tied to low-pressure systems such as tropical cyclones, and it is measured without counting waves.
Its main driver is fast wind pushing water toward the coast over a long stretch of sea, helped by the air pressure drop, tide timing and shallow water.
As climate change brings more intense extreme weather and higher seas, storm surges are expected to put coastal populations at greater risk.

facts.label: Other names
facts.value: Storm flood, tidal surge, or storm tide

facts.label: Pressure effect
facts.value: About 10 mm rise per millibar of pressure drop

facts.label: Wave run-up
facts.value: Can exceed twice the wave height

facts.label: Shallow surge zones
facts.value: Gulf of Mexico coast and the Bay of Bengal

items.prompt: A major storm's air pressure is 100 millibars below normal. Leaving wind aside, about how much does the sea rise from the pressure drop alone?

options.label: About 1 centimetre
About 10 centimetres
About 1 metre
About 10 metres

items.explain: The sea rises roughly 10 mm for each millibar of pressure drop, so a 100 millibar drop gives about a 1 m rise.

items.prompt: The same hurricane heads for two coasts: one with deep water close to shore, one with a wide, shallow shelf. Which gets the higher surge?

options.label: The shallow shelf, where the water has less room to spread
The deep coast, where bigger waves pile up
Both get the same surge from the same storm
The deep coast, where more water is available

items.explain: On a wide, shallow shelf the surge has less room to disperse and is driven ashore; deep water lets it spread down and away, giving lower surge but bigger waves.

items.prompt: A storm grows to twice its earlier width while its winds stay the same. What happens to its surge height?

options.label: It stays the same, since only wind speed counts
It drops, since the storm's energy spreads out
It rises, since its area grows faster than its edge
It halves, since the water spreads over more coast

items.explain: Doubling a storm's diameter doubles its perimeter but quadruples its area, so the surge has proportionally less edge to dissipate through and ends up higher.

items.prompt: In the Northern Hemisphere, Earth's rotation bends a storm's currents so they meet the shore more head-on. What does that do to the surge?

options.label: Weakens it, by slowing the currents
Has no effect on the surge
Turns it into a series of waves
Strengthens it, by aiming water at the shore

items.explain: The Coriolis effect bends currents; when the bend brings them more perpendicular to the shore it amplifies the surge, and when it turns them away it lessens it.

items.prompt: A town sits at the head of a tidal estuary. A hurricane dumps heavy rain inland while pushing seawater toward the coast. Why does water there rise extra high?

options.label: Rain makes seawater expand as it cools
Ocean surge meets river runoff coming downstream
The estuary drains faster during storms
Heavy rain raises the air pressure

items.explain: Rain floods streams and rivers, and that water flowing down the estuary collides with storm-driven seawater surging in, raising the level near the head of the estuary.

items.prompt: When forecasters give a storm surge's height, what exactly are they measuring?

options.label: The height of the biggest wave
The total water depth at the shore
How far the water reaches inland
The rise above normal tide, not counting waves

items.explain: Storm surge is measured as the rise in water level above the normal tidal level, and waves are not included.

paragraphs.heading: What a storm surge is
paragraphs.text: A storm surge is a rise of seawater onto the coast, most often linked to low-pressure weather systems such as tropical cyclones. It also goes by the names storm flood, tidal surge or storm tide. It is measured as how far the water climbs above the normal tide level, leaving waves out. The biggest weather driver is fast wind pushing water toward the coast over a long stretch of sea.

paragraphs.heading: Wind and spin
paragraphs.text: At least five processes can change water levels during a storm. Wind setup is the rise of water on the downwind shore and its drop on the upwind shore, as the storm blows water to one side of the basin. Strong winds also drive surface currents at a 45° angle to the wind, through an effect called the Ekman spiral. Earth's rotation adds the Coriolis effect: currents curve right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern. When that bend turns currents more squarely toward the shore it can raise the surge, and when it turns them away it lowers it.

paragraphs.heading: Low pressure lifts the sea
paragraphs.text: Under a tropical cyclone, the open ocean rises where air pressure is low and falls where it is high. The water rises just enough to balance the drop in air pressure, so the total pressure at some level below the surface stays the same. The estimate is about 10 mm of extra sea level for each millibar the pressure falls. So a big storm whose pressure falls by 100 millibars would lift the water by about 1.0 m from this effect alone.

paragraphs.heading: Waves and rain
paragraphs.text: Waves are powered by the wind but act differently from the wind-driven currents. Out at sea they move little water, but near shore, breaking in lines roughly parallel to the beach, they carry a lot of water landward. That moving water can run up a sloping beach above the average water line, sometimes higher than twice the wave's height before it broke. In estuaries, rain matters most: hurricanes can drop as much as 300 mm in 24 hours, runoff quickly floods streams and rivers, and that river water meets the surge pushing in from the sea, raising the level near the head of the estuary.

paragraphs.heading: The shape of the seabed
paragraphs.text: The shape and depth of the sea floor and the coast also matter. A narrow shelf with deep water close in tends to give a lower surge but bigger, stronger waves, while a wide, shallow shelf gives a higher surge with smaller waves. In deep water the surge can spread down and away from the hurricane, but on a shallow, gently sloping shelf it has little room and the wind drives it ashore. Florida shows both: off Palm Beach the water is 91 metres deep just 3 km out, while on the Gulf side the Floridian Plateau's edge may sit over 160 kilometres from shore, and very shallow Florida Bay gets higher surges with smaller waves.

paragraphs.heading: Land, size and the future
paragraphs.text: Land lying less than a few metres above sea level is especially exposed to surge flooding. Storm size counts as well: if a storm doubles in diameter, its perimeter doubles but its area grows fourfold. With less perimeter for the water to spread out through, the surge ends up higher. As extreme weather grows more intense and seas rise with climate change, storm surges are expected to threaten coastal people more. Communities can respond with flood barriers, dunes or mangroves, better building practices, and early warning, education and evacuation plans.
